A smart ring prototype developed by University of California engineers appears to have cracked one of the holy grails of health wearables: measuring blood glucose without a needle. The data is sent to a companion app on a paired iPhone.

While existing smart rings rely purely on biophysical data extracted from sensors — like those embedded in the Apple Watch — this one tracks chemical biomarkers by analyzing sweat……

Today's smart rings work in exactly the same way as the Apple Watch, using the very same sensors. These gather a fairly wide range of data, including resting heart rate, heart rate variability, respiration rate, body temperature, cardiovascular age, activity, sleep cycles and more.

But adding molecular sensors on top of existing sensors dramatically increases the amount of health data that can be collected. According to CNET, users don't even need to exercise and sweat — the technology draws sweat from the skin.

Engineers at the University of California, San Diego believe they have developed the first smart ring to track chemical biomarkers using sweat from the fingertip. While currently just a prototype, it demonstrates the potential for future smart rings to continuously monitor the body at a molecular level, without relying purely on biophysical data. In a paper published in Nature Communications on July 23, the engineering team said this new smart ring uses sweat to continuously monitor up to four of the following biochemical markers: glucose, ketones, vitamin C, uric acid, lactate and alcohol levels.

The ring could be particularly useful for people with Type 1 diabetes.

Testing showed its accuracy was very close to that of invasive continuous glucose monitors and blood tests.

The prototype ring is rather bulky and only has a 12-hour battery life, but a commercial version is expected to make significant improvements in both areas. I'd love to see what Apple engineers could do with this technology.
